Oil Climbs as Fighting Flares in Middle East, Ukraine
 
Plus, a Starbucks-Chipotle merger that wasn’t, and credit scores for mortgages are changing
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
An air traffic control tower at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. AGENCE FRANCE-PRESSE/GETTY IMAGES
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Oil rose. Brent crude futures climbed 1.8% to cross $106 a barrel. Yemen’s Houthis fired a missile over the weekend that hit Riyadh’s airport, highlighting the threat the Iran-backed militants pose to the oil producer’s infrastructure. In Ukraine, meanwhile, Russian strikes hit energy facilities across the country despite President Trump’s declaration that the sides had reached an “energy ceasefire.”

 

Stocks were mixed. The flare-ups in the Middle East and Ukraine weighed on stocks, with the S&P 500 off by 0.06% and Nasdaq index declining 0.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended 0.4% higher, however.

 

Chipotle fell and Starbucks rose. Starbucks said it would not bid for Chipotle, following speculation about a possible deal, pushing its shares up 1.7%. Investors in Chipotle, which has been grappling with rising labor costs and food-price inflation, appeared less pleased that the deal talk was off: Its shares dropped 3.8%.

 

SWI Group rose. The Amsterdam-listed company, which operates bitcoin-mining operations once part of Sam Bankman-Fried’s bankrupt FTX, raised around $900 million to upgrade and expand its data centers. The company plans to offer computing infrastructure to big tech companies focused on AI. Its shares rose more than 16%.

 
 
 
CONTENT FROM: GOLDMAN SACHS
 
 
Will European gas prices keep rising this winter?
 
Europe's energy markets are facing a challenging winter due to ongoing Middle East supply disruptions. European liquid natural gas prices have risen in recent months and are projected to remain high subject to the pace of Middle East export recovery.

One Big Story

 
 
Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte. KEVIN LAMARQUE/REUTERS
 

Fair Isaac’s FICO score has long been the near-universal measure of creditworthiness when people apply for mortgages. No more. The Federal Housing Finance Agency, which oversees Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae, now allows mortgage lenders to use VantageScore, a metric co-developed by the U.S.’s three big credit-reporting companies. VantageScores typically come in higher than FICO scores, which should lead to more mortgage approvals—but also possibly higher default risk.

• An index of small-business optimism, also for September, is expected in the morning.

 

• Bank earnings season kicks into high gear, with reports from JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo and Citigroup before the bell.
